strengths: The paper makes a clear conceptual contribution by separating visual (in-image) bias from textual prompt bias: prior counterfactual VLM benchmarks (PhD-ccs, VLind-Bench, HallusionBench) embed biased statements in the prompt, whereas VLMBias uses neutral, objective counting/identification questions with bias cues injected into the image, which cleanly isolates the proposed phenomenon.

The benchmark is broad and systematic: 7 domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, game boards, optical illusions, novel patterned grids) with ~1,400 counterfactual images at 3 resolutions, covering both photo-realistic and abstract (code-generated) images, which strengthens the claim that the effect is general rather than an artifact of one image type.

The experimental design includes good controls: a sanity check showing 100% accuracy on unmodified originals establishes that models know the subjects and that failures are specific to counterfactuals; analysis of bias-aligned vs. random errors (Fig. 4) supports the memorization hypothesis; the from-scratch patterned grid controls for internet-memorized patterns.

Several findings are interesting and actionable for the community: thinking models offer little benefit (and are more hurt by in-image text), debiased/double-check prompts help by only +1.9/+2.7 points, and adversarial in-image text further degrades accuracy.

The data generation pipeline (LLM ideation, text-to-image generation, SVG/code-based rendering, human review) is well documented with prompts and quality-control procedures in a detailed appendix, and code/data are stated to be released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: A key confound is not fully resolved: VLMs are known to be generally poor at counting and fine-grained visual tasks (the paper itself cites [44]). Low accuracy on counterfactual boards, Sudoku/Go grids, and patterned grids (e.g., 2.26% on game boards) may reflect generic counting blindness rather than knowledge-driven bias; the paper only partially disentangles these (Q3 and grid experiments help, but per-domain bias-attribution is uneven).

The evaluation lacks statistical rigor: results appear to be from single runs at temperature 1.0 with no variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests, which is concerning given some reported margins are small (e.g., +2-point prompt effects).

The benchmark is narrow in scope regarding subjects: only 3 car brands, 2 shoe brands, 20 flags, 2 board games for chess-like tasks; conclusions about 'VLMs are biased' rest on a limited set of popular entities, and no open-weight or smaller VLMs are tested (only 5 proprietary frontier models), limiting generality.

Generated counterfactual images may be unnatural or artifact-laden (multi-legged animals, modified logos), and the paper acknowledges difficulty controlling image-generation models; there is no human performance baseline on the counterfactual images to confirm the modifications are as perceptually obvious to humans as assumed.

The paper is diagnostic only: it documents the failure mode but offers no mitigation, analysis of internal representations, or intervention beyond simple prompts, which limits its contribution beyond prior 'VLMs are blind' style work.

Presentation issues: duplicated references ([50]/[51], [15]/[16]), a code link left incomplete in the abstract, some inconsistencies (e.g., 'Adadias', the appendix L.5 text ends abruptly), and parts of the related-work comparison in Table 1 (e.g., 'n/a' leaderboard entries) feel like ad hoc benchmark positioning.

strengths: The benchmark construction is systematic and unusually careful for this genre: automated CF-image generation pipelines, explicit ground-truth/bias-answer definitions per task, three image resolutions, and a sanity-check stage confirming 100% accuracy on unmodified images, which is necessary before attributing CF failures to bias.

Good coverage: 7 diverse domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, board games, optical illusions, patterned grids), 1,392 CF images, and 5 recent SOTA VLMs including both thinking and non-thinking models.

The bias-aligned error analysis (75.70% of wrong answers match the predefined biased answer) and the patterned-grid task (created from scratch, so no Internet prior) are nice controls that partially disentangle memorized bias from generic failure.

Useful ablations: in-image adversarial text injection (accuracy drops further, more for thinking models) and helpful-prompt experiments (debiased/double-check prompting gains only ~+2 points), which give the paper more than just a headline number.
Code, data, and prompts are released, and the appendix documents the generation pipelines and quality-control procedures in detail.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core finding — VLMs answer from memorized priors and ignore fine-grained counterfactual image edits — is well anticipated by HallusionBench, VLind-Bench, PhD-ccs, and especially 'VLMs are Blind' [44], which already showed severe counting failures. The paper is largely an extension/repackaging of these ideas with neutral prompts instead of biased Y/N questions, and the headline result (17% accuracy) is not surprising.

A residual confound between 'bias' and 'general counting inability' is not fully resolved. VLMs are known to be poor at counting and at fine-grained perception; several task results (e.g., 2.26% on board-game rows/columns) could reflect base capability limits amplified by any plausible answer, and the paper does not provide a matched 'neutral prior' control task with comparable counting difficulty to isolate the bias effect quantitatively.

Generated images are themselves a validity risk: CF animals/logos produced by text-to-image models may contain artifacts (unnatural limb placement, inconsistent logo geometry) that are hard even for humans to parse, and human quality review is only described briefly with no reported inter-annotator agreement or acceptance statistics. Some reported numbers (e.g., 0.44% on car logos) may partly measure image realism rather than bias.

The optical illusion task yields ~50% (chance-level) accuracy, making the 'bias' interpretation weak there — models that cannot do the task at all would also score ~50%; the paper's own Sonnet-3.7 result (better on CF than originals) suggests the task measures noise as much as bias.

Evaluation protocol is thin on statistics: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple runs (temperature=1.0 means answers are stochastic; single-run accuracies on small per-task subsets, e.g., 84 board images, are noisy). Some differences cited as meaningful (e.g., thinking vs. non-thinking models) are small.

Significance is diagnostic rather than constructive: the paper documents failures but offers no analysis of mechanism (e.g., encoder-vs-LLM attribution is only mentioned as future work in the discussion), limiting its impact beyond anecdotally memorable examples like the 4-striped Adidas logo.

Several presentation issues: duplicate references ([15]/[16], [50]/[51]), a truncated code link in the abstract, LaTeX artifacts ('textbf' in Figure 17), and claims like 'fully automated on 6 of 7 tasks' that overstate automation given the extensive manual editing described in the appendices (e.g., manual logo placement).

strengths: The core experimental design is a genuine advance over prior bias benchmarks (PhD-ccs, VLind-Bench, HallusionBench): bias cues are injected into the image rather than the prompt, and questions are neutral, objective counting/identification tasks. This cleanly addresses the open question of whether VLM failures stem from the image or the textual prompt.

Excellent methodological controls: a sanity check establishes 100% recognition of unmodified subjects (validating that failures on counterfactuals are attributable to bias); a bias-aligned vs. correct vs. other-error decomposition (Fig. 4) shows ~75.7% of answers match the predefined bias, strongly supporting the bias hypothesis over random visual confusion.

The patterned-grid task is a particularly clever control: the pattern is novel (not on the Internet), yet VLMs still default to the global pattern 43.45% of the time, showing the failure is not purely memorization of internet knowledge.

Systematic and transparent benchmark construction: 1,392 CF images across 7 domains, three resolutions, multiple prompt phrasings, documented generation pipelines (App. C–I), all prompts released, code and data made available — good reproducibility.

The adversarial in-image text experiment (Sec. 4.7) and the mitigation experiments (Sec. 4.8) add actionable findings, e.g., thinking models are more susceptible to in-image text, and debiasing/double-check prompts yield only +1.87/+2.70 points.
Clear writing, informative figures (Figs. 1, 3, 5), and honest limitations section discussing generator-quality confounds and inability to test tool-using VLMs.
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the headline finding — VLMs override visual evidence with memorized priors on counterfactual images — is consistent with a substantial line of prior work (HallusionBench, PhD-ccs, VLind-Bench, 'VLMs are Blind', BlindTest). The contribution is a cleaner measurement protocol and a new benchmark rather than a fundamentally new insight or mitigation.

An important confound is only partially resolved: VLMs are known to be poor at counting and fine-grained perception in general (their own Ref. [44]). The near-0% accuracy on game boards (Tab. 9, 2.26%) suggests these failures may largely reflect baseline blindness rather than bias; the bias-aligned error analysis mitigates but does not fully eliminate this concern, and a non-patterned counting control for the grid task is missing.

Evaluation protocol limitations: each configuration appears to be evaluated once at temperature 1.0, with no repetitions, variance estimates, or significance tests; conclusions drawn from small per-task differences (e.g., +2 points from prompting) could be within run-to-run noise.

Model coverage is narrow: five closed-source frontier APIs only, no open-weight VLMs, and no access to internal representations. The interesting question the authors themselves pose (does the vision encoder perceive the change, or is the LLM overriding it?) is left as speculation.

Some tasks have limited scope (e.g., only 5 logo brands, 20 flags), and generated counterfactual images (e.g., 5-legged animals) may be off-distribution in ways beyond the intended manipulation; human review is described but inter-annotator agreement or validation with human accuracy is not reported.

Claims such as 'thinking models hallucinate more' rest on a single aggregate comparison and would benefit from more rigorous analysis; the abstract's framing ('VLMs are Biased') is somewhat stronger than what a benchmark-only study can establish causally.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: unlike prior bias benchmarks (PhD-ccs, VLind-Bench, HallusionBench) that embed biased statements in the prompt, VLMBias isolates image-driven bias using neutral prompts and objective counting tasks, making the source of failure unambiguous.

Well-designed benchmark: 1,392 counterfactual images across 7 diverse domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, game boards, optical illusions, patterned grids), with systematic construction pipelines (SOTA generators for photo-realistic tasks, code-generated abstract images), explicit bias/ground-truth definitions, and a sanity check showing 100% accuracy on unmodified images that grounds the causal claim.

Unusually thorough evaluation: five SOTA commercial VLMs plus GPT-5, Grok-4, open-source models of varying sizes, and counting-specialized/pointing VLMs; controls for image resolution (A.18), generator–evaluator model-family confounds (A.17), multiple runs for stability (A.11), prompting mitigations, few-shot experiments, and tool-use analysis.

The linear-probing experiment (A.8) is a highlight: SigLIP features classify leg counts at 95.26% while the full VLM performs at chance with 99.43% bias rate, providing a mechanistic explanation that the language model overrides visual evidence rather than the encoder failing.

Additional valuable analyses: background-removal experiment (+21.09 accuracy, −40.58 bias) that pins bias to background context, in-image adversarial text injection, reasoning-length vs. accuracy (overthinking) analysis, a 78-participant human study confirming the CF images are perceivable, and evidence of inverse scaling on bias rate.
High reproducibility: code and data released, prompts and model access details fully specified in appendices, and generation pipelines documented per task.
weaknesses: Some tasks conflate general visual-counting weakness with knowledge bias. E.g., game-board row/column counting at 2.26% and Sudoku/Go at 0% (A.5) likely reflects low-level counting blindness (cf. 'VLMs are blind') rather than memorized-answer bias, yet these are folded into the headline 'bias' narrative; the distinction is not cleanly quantified per task.

Findings that VLMs are poor at counting and fail on counterfactual/modified images overlap with known results (Rahmanzadehgervi et al., ViLP, Bitton-Guetta et al.), so the core phenomenon is somewhat incremental; the novelty lies mainly in benchmark design, the neutral-prompt setup, and the background/probing analyses.

Photo-realistic CF images are produced by generative models, and even with the A.17 family analysis, subtle generation artifacts or implausible anatomy could independently affect model behavior; the human study covers only the animal task, so image realism is not verified across all domains.

The bias metric assumes a single canonical 'bias' answer per question, which is reasonable for logos/flags but weaker for tasks where multiple non-biased errors are possible; some per-subtask tables (e.g., 20 flags, 5 brands) yield small sample sizes for the sub-analyses.

Some inconsistencies and typos remain (e.g., 'Pogendorff' vs. Poggendorff, tool-use accuracy deltas reported differently in the text (+1.9 from 23.18) vs. Table 4 context, Table 16 caption repeating 36.02% twice), and Sec. 4.5 mixes reasoning-token and reasoning-time metrics across models, complicating the overthinking claim.

The optical illusion task largely shows random-chance performance and contradictory per-model behavior (Sonnet-3.7 better on CF than original), which the paper attributes to bias but does not fully explain.

strengths: The benchmark (VLMBias) is systematically constructed across 7 domains with a mix of photo-realistic (generator-based) and programmatic (SVG/script) images, and includes a human quality-control step for counterfactual images.

The evaluation is broad: 5 frontier closed-source VLMs plus recent models (GPT-5, Grok-4), 4 open-source VLMs, and specialized counting/pointing models (Molmo, Moondream), with sanity checks on unmodified images (100% accuracy) that help rule out trivial explanations for the failures.

Several supporting analyses are valuable: the linear-probing experiment showing the SigLIP encoder encodes leg counts (95.26%) while the full VLM fails (49.71%), the background-removal ablation, the in-image adversarial text injection, the 5-run consistency/overconfidence analysis, and a small human study confirming the images are perceivable by humans given sufficient time.
The paper is well organized with an extensive appendix covering data-generation pipelines, prompts, and qualitative results, and code/data are released.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the central finding. That VLMs favor language priors/memorized answers over visual evidence is well established (HallusionBench, VLind-Bench, PhD-ccs, ViLP, Whoops, VALSE, BlindTest/'VLMs are blind'). The contribution is largely a re-instantiation of this known phenomenon with neutral prompts and counting questions; Table 1's claimed differentiators are incremental rather than fundamental.

Attribution of failures to 'bias from prior knowledge' is overclaimed. Many failures (counting rows on a 19x19 Go board, counting chess pieces, stripes at low resolution) are consistent with the previously documented poor fine-grained perception of VLMs rather than prior-knowledge bias specifically. The background-removal gain (+21.09) could equally reflect image simplification/crop quality rather than 'background cues triggering bias'. The paper itself cites VLMs' low-level vision deficits, which undercuts the bias-centric narrative.

Several internal inconsistencies and sloppy details undermine confidence: Table 16's caption reads '36.02% vs. 36.02%'; the text reports o4-mini tool-use gains as both '+4.83' and '+1.9'; Table 20 text says VLM counterfactual accuracy of '2.21%' vs. '2.12%' elsewhere; a malformed 'textbf(c)' appears in Figure 22; the optical illusion task is included in 'counting' aggregates though it is a Y/N task.

The 'decreasing popularity' ordering of the 7 domains is asserted but never quantified (no measurement of subject frequency in training data), so the claim that biases stem from the text corpus is speculative; the in-image text experiment (A.9) is suggestive but weak evidence.

Some results weaken the headline claim without adequate discussion: GPT-5 scores 84.72% on chess-piece counting, pointing VLMs (small models) reach 36.02%, and few-shot + hint boosts GPT-4.1 to 60.81% — indicating the 'VLMs are strongly biased' framing is model- and protocol-dependent.

The benchmark's practical significance is unclear: counterfactual images of 5-legged animals and 4-striped Adidas logos are artificial adversarial constructions, and the paper provides no evidence these failure modes matter for real applications; no mitigation beyond minor prompt engineering is proposed.

Reproducibility concerns: results depend on specific, quickly deprecating API model versions and default settings (temperature=1.0, reasoning_effort=medium) that are not standardizable; the human study covers only the animal task with 78 participants, so the human baseline does not validate the other six domains.

strengths: The paper presents a comprehensive, well-organized benchmark (VLMBias) with 1,392 counterfactual images across 7 diverse domains (animals, logos, flags, chess, board games, optical illusions, and a novel patterned-grid task), plus background-removal and in-image-text subsets totaling 4,176 images.

The central experimental design is clean and convincing: sanity checks confirm VLMs achieve 100% on unmodified images, isolating the effect of the counterfactual modification, and neutral prompts rule out prompt-induced bias that plagued prior benchmarks (Tab. 1 comparison is well positioned).

Analysis goes well beyond headline numbers: linear probing shows vision encoders already encode the relevant information (95.26%) while the full VLM fails, the background-removal experiment (+21.09 accuracy, -40.58 bias rate) identifies a likely cause, and the reasoning-token analysis reveals a non-monotonic accuracy curve with overthinking effects.

Broad model coverage (5 SOTA commercial VLMs, GPT-5/Grok-4, 4 open-source VLMs, 3 pointing VLMs) plus robustness checks (5-run stability, resolution ablation, cross-family generation controls) and a human study (n=78, timed conditions) that validates task perceptibility and provides a strong human baseline.
Clear writing, extensive qualitative examples, detailed reproducibility materials (prompts, generation pipelines, model access details), and released code/data.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the paper substantially extends known findings — VLMs' fine-grained visual failures (Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 'VLMs are blind'), counterfactual hallucination benchmarks (Whoops, HallusionBench, ViLP), and language-prior work (VLind-Bench). The main new elements are the neutral-prompt design and objective counting tasks, which are incremental over this line of work.

There are potential confounds the paper does not fully rule out: many failures (e.g., 0% on Go/Sudoku row counting, 2.12% on animal legs) may reflect well-documented general weaknesses in counting and fine-grained spatial perception rather than 'bias' per se; separating bias-driven from capability-driven failure is only partially addressed (the patterned-grid task helps, but bias and blindness are entangled in most tasks).

Image quality concerns from generative CF editing (acknowledged in Limitations: Gemini-2.0 Flash sometimes fails to modify logos correctly) mean some human-reviewed images may still contain artifacts; the human study covers only the animal task, so perceptibility of modifications in other domains is not validated with humans.

Some inconsistencies and sloppiness undermine polish: Table 16 caption states '36.02% vs. 36.02%' (typo), the Maserati ground truth ('Correct answer: 5, Expected bias: 3') is inconsistent with other entries, minor errors like 'textbf' leakage, and the optical-illusion task is Y/N rather than counting despite being aggregated into the 17.05% counting headline.

The 'inverse scaling' claim is based on only 4 open-source models of uneven training quality and is weaker than the evidence presented; bias-rate comparisons across open/closed models conflate model size with data and training differences.

Practical significance is arguable: the benchmark is diagnostic rather than actionable — no mitigation is shown to work well (helpful prompts add only +2.7, tools +1.9), and it is unclear how training or evaluation pipelines would use VLMBias to reduce bias.
